correctness.rationale: Both divisor sums are multiplicative, with σ*(p^a)=1+p^a, σ^(e)(p^a)=sum_{d|a}p^d. For a=ℓ² this becomes (1+p^a)(1+q)=q(p+p^ℓ+p^a), hence q(p+p^ℓ−1)=p^a+1. Let D=p+p^ℓ−1; if p>2, odd ℓ gives p^a+1 mod D =1−(p−1)^ℓ, a nonzero residue whose absolute value is strictly below D, impossible to divide. For p=2, x^ℓ+1 divides x^(ℓ²)+1 (x=2), and quotient Φ_(2ℓ²)(2) must be prime, with converse immediate. Independently computed small quotient values and primality for ℓ=3,5,7; uniform proof is elementary congruence, not a finite test.

value.rationale: The result explains why the largest highlighted known equality example has exponent 49 and isolates a natural infinite subfamily of a published infinitude problem, with precise structural obstruction for all odd p. It does not claim infinitely many cyclotomic primes or settle the full equality problem.

final_claim: For odd prime ℓ and distinct primes p,q, unitary-divisor sum σ*(p^(ℓ²)q) equals exponential-divisor sum σ^(e)(p^(ℓ²)q) iff p=2 and q=Φ_(2ℓ²)(2) is prime. At ℓ=3,5 values 57 and 1016801 are composite; ℓ=7 gives prime 4363953127297 and the known solution 2^49 times that prime.
limitations: Only p^(ℓ²)q, ℓ odd prime, p≠q; no assertion for general exponent vectors.
Exact known ℓ=7 example explicitly credited, not a new example.
